newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater counsel wants more cooperation in probe.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater counsel wants more cooperation in probe.

text.p: Whitewater Independent Counsel Kenneth Starr said Monday his probe of the failed Arkansas land deal had been hampered by lack of cooperation by people with relevant information, whom he urged to come forward.
Starr, who spoke to reporters before a speech to the Economic Club of Detroit, declined to identify those who were not cooperating but said their help would make the investigation move more quickly.

"The difficulty in this investigation has been getting at the truth as promptly as I would like," Starr said. "The more forthcoming and the more cooperative individuals who have relevant information are with this investigation, the sooner the investigation will be over."

The most striking example of noncooperation so far has been Susan McDougal, who went to jail on contempt-of-court charges in September for refusing testify before a grand jury about President Clinton's role in the saga.
McDougal, a former business partner of Clinton and his wife, was found guilty of four counts of fraud in the first Whitewater trial earlier this year and sentenced to two years in prison.
She could serve up to 17 months more for contempt but has stood by her refusal to testify. She says prosecutors want her to invent evidence against Clinton.

McDougal's former husband, Jim McDougal, who was convicted of a string of fraud and conspiracy charges related to the Whitewater project, has agreed to cooperate with the investigation. He faced up to 84 years in prison, but his sentencing was postponed until Nov. 18.
In his rare appearance before reporters, Starr declined to say whether he would recommend a more lenient sentence for Jim McDougal or to comment on other matters directly linked to the investigation.

Asked if it could be wrapped up in the next year or if it could take five more years, Starr said he hoped the duration would be closer to one year. But he noted that if more criminal charges were brought, preparations for new trials could take a long time.
A second trial for former Arkansas Gov. Jim Guy Tucker, convicted on several fraud and conspiracy charges in the first trial, has been delayed because of his health problems.
Starr said the investigation so far had cost taxpayers about $9 million but his team was working to hold costs down.
He rejected Democratic charges that he was conducting a partisan campaign. "It is, in short, about public trust and civic virtue," he said of the investigation.
